cases.why: A direct mailbox message for one session. The trailing segment is the SESSION TOKEN, not the name: a session name may contain characters a subject cannot carry, so both ends derive a token and must derive the SAME one.
A tool call addressed to one extension tool. Note the `call` segment — a reader that builds `.tool.<ext>.<name>` publishes to a subject nothing subscribes to.
Progress frames for one in-flight call, keyed by call id so a turn can subscribe before the first frame arrives.
A lazily-resolved prompt variable, addressed by extension and name.
The durable event stream a reconnecting client replays. Keyed by session TOKEN, like the mailbox.
Session-list changes for a tenant. One subject per tenant, not per session.
An interrupt aimed at one extension. Lives under `ctl.`, which a reader that assumes a flat layout will miss.
An interrupt aimed at every extension of a tenant.
A session lifecycle event, addressed by KIND so a subscriber picks the ones it cares about instead of filtering in code.
A call hook, addressed by extension AND hook name.
An event hook: addressed by hook name ALONE, unlike a call hook. Asymmetric on purpose and easy to get wrong.
Config changes for one extension. No trailing wildcard here — the subscriber watches the extension's own subject.
One channel message. The topic may contain slashes and dots and is passed through unchanged.
A consumer derives the tenant from the SUBJECT, never the payload: a publisher that lies in its payload must not reach another tenant.
A foreign subject yields NO tenant rather than a guessed one.
A bare `easybus.<tenant>` prefix is not a subject with a tenant.

why: Every subject is built four times (Go, TypeScript, Python, Rust) and a wrong one fails silently: the message is published to a subject nobody subscribes to, or read from one nobody writes. Nothing errors — the feature just does not work. These are the exact strings, so a divergence in any language is a failing test rather than a missing message.
